62753713
1. 1926 to August 1929, build a stake. Save a third of your pay and buy leaders like RCA and GM on margin, but never borrow more than you put in or a normal dip wipes you out. Sell everything by Labor Day 1929. The Dow peaks at 381 the next day.

2. September 1929 to July 1932, short the collapse. Short the froth like RCA and the investment trusts, which go nearly to zero. Cover in mid November, sit out the 48 percent rally into April 1930, then short again until the July 1932 bottom, down 89 percent. Never lever your shorts, since sharp rallies hit on the way down.

3. Guard the cash. About 9000 banks fail and there is no FDIC until 1934, so use Postal Savings and Treasuries. Falling prices make each dollar buy a third more by 1933. Skip gold coins, since FDR forces you to sell at 20.67 an ounce in 1933, then reprices gold at 35. Own gold miners like Homestake instead.

4. 1932 to 1938, buy the bottom and short the relapse. Go long in July 1932, and the Dow nearly quintuples by March 1937. Sell there and short again, because it nearly halves by spring 1938.

5. 1942 to 1946, the war trade. Sit in Treasuries until the April 1942 low, when the war news is darkest. Then do what John Templeton did in 1939 and buy a broad basket of beaten down, even bankrupt, companies. He roughly quadrupled borrowed money that way. Cash out by mid 1946.

Throughout, keep a job that survives the Depression, carry no debt from 1930 to 1933, and stay humble. Jesse Livermore reportedly made 100 million dollars shorting the crash and was bankrupt by 1934.

Rough math with perfect discipline. About 1500 dollars saved becomes 3 to 4 thousand by 1929, 10 thousand by 1932, 40 thousand by 1937, and low six figures by 1946, which is seven figures today before taxes.
